examples.name: hello
examples.title: Hello, Garnet
examples.description: The canonical hello-world (`@caps()`, pure compute + stdout).
examples.source:
# hello.garnet — the canonical Garnet hello-world.
#
# `@caps()` declares the program needs no OS authority (pure compute + stdout).
#
# Run:   garnet run examples/hello.garnet
# Check: garnet check examples/hello.garnet

@caps()
def main() {
  println("Hello from Garnet!")
  0
}

examples.name: undeclared_memory_tier
examples.title: Undeclared memory tier
examples.description: `@caps()` reaches `memory::working`; `check` reports the missing `mem` and `run` traps before the store exists (D-04).
examples.source:
# undeclared_memory_tier.garnet — a memory tier is authority, and this
# program never asked for it.
#
# `@caps()` declares no authority at all. The body then reaches for
# `memory::working`, one of the four memory tiers that require `@caps(mem)`
# (D-04, ADR 0011). Two independent gates stop it:
#
#   garnet check  — check.caps_coverage: `main` does not declare `mem` but
#                   transitively calls `memory::working` which requires it
#   garnet run    — runtime trap before the store is created, on both the
#                   interpreter and the VM
#
# Add `mem` to the `@caps(...)` list and `garnet diff-caps` reports the
# expansion. The fix is one word; the point is that it must be written down.

@caps()
def main() {
  let scratch = memory::working("scratch")
  scratch.push("never reached")
  0
}
examples.output:
runtime error: capability: `memory::working` requires @caps(mem), not declared in the calling chain
exit 1
